legend: While looking at the kitchen fridge, the little boy Tyler noticed magnets with symbols, that can be aligned into a string s%%ZSMJ0%%.

Tyler likes strings, and especially those that are lexicographically smaller than another string, t%%ZSMJ1%%. After playing with magnets on the fridge, he is wondering, how many distinct strings can be composed out of letters of string s%%ZSMJ2%% by rearranging them, so that the resulting string is lexicographically smaller than the string t%%ZSMJ3%%? Tyler is too young, so he can't answer this question. The alphabet Tyler uses is very large, so for your convenience he has already replaced the same letters in s%%ZSMJ4%% and t%%ZSMJ5%% to the same integers, keeping that different letters have been replaced to different integers.
We call a string x%%ZSMJ6%% lexicographically smaller than a string y%%ZSMJ7%% if one of the followings conditions is fulfilled:

There exists such position of symbol m%%ZSMJ8%% that is presented in both strings, so that before m%%ZSMJ9%%-th symbol the strings are equal, and the m%%ZSMJ10%%-th symbol of string x%%ZSMJ11%% is smaller than m%%ZSMJ12%%-th symbol of string y%%ZSMJ13%%.
String x%%ZSMJ14%% is the prefix of string y%%ZSMJ15%% and x≠y%%ZSMJ16%%.
Because the answer can be too large, print it modulo 998244353%%ZSMJ17%%.
input: The first line contains two integers n%%ZSMJ18%% and m%%ZSMJ19%% (1≤n,m≤200000%%ZSMJ20%%) — the lengths of strings s%%ZSMJ21%% and t%%ZSMJ22%% respectively.
The second line contains n%%ZSMJ23%% integers s1,s2,s3,…,sn%%ZSMJ24%% (1≤si≤200000%%ZSMJ25%%) — letters of the string s%%ZSMJ26%%.
The third line contains m%%ZSMJ27%% integers t1,t2,t3,…,tm%%ZSMJ28%% (1≤ti≤200000%%ZSMJ29%%) — letters of the string t%%ZSMJ30%%.
output: Print a single number — the number of strings lexicographically smaller than t%%ZSMJ31%% that can be obtained by rearranging the letters in s%%ZSMJ32%%, modulo 998244353%%ZSMJ33%%.
note: In the first example, the strings we are interested in are [122]%%ZSMJ34%% and [212]%%ZSMJ35%%. The string [221]%%ZSMJ36%% is lexicographically larger than the string [2121]%%ZSMJ37%%, so we don't count it.
In the second example, all strings count except [4321]%%ZSMJ38%%, so the answer is 4!−1=23%%ZSMJ39%%.
In the third example, only the string [1112]%%ZSMJ40%% counts.
